`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass field default evaluated when the module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` created in the process gets the same timestamp (the process start time), not the creation time. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
to_dict/from_dict round-trip breaks across Celery JSON serialization

`to_dict()` returns a `datetime` for `queued`, which is passed as a Celery task kwarg (`assignment_source_dict` in sync_group_assignee_outbound). With a JSON serializer this either raises a serialization error or, if coerced, arrives in the worker as a string, so `from_dict` will construct an `AssignmentSource` whose `queued` is a `str` (no validation catches it since `cls(**input_dict)` accepts any type). Serialize `queued` to ISO format in `to_dict` and parse it back in `from_dict`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
New `assignment_source` kwarg may break existing sync_assignee_outbound implementations

The task now always passes `assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound`. Any integration implementation whose signature does not accept `**kwargs`/`assignment_source` (e.g. third-party or plugin-based installations, and `IssueBasicIntegration` subclasses) will raise TypeError at runtime, silently failing assignee syncs after retries. Verify all implementations accept the kwarg or pass it only when present.

where_should_sync does not forward assignment source

`where_should_sync` calls `should_sync(key)` without a `sync_source`, so inbound paths that use it (e.g. `sync_status_inbound`, `sync_group_assignee_inbound`'s org filtering) cannot suppress cycles for status syncs. The newly added `assignment_source` parameter on `sync_status_outbound` is therefore never populated anywhere, leaving the status-sync cycle unaddressed despite the API change.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is no longer instantiable

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with only `pass`, but StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). Since the class leaves them unimplemented, `Detector.detector_handler` -> `group_type.detector_handler(self)` will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...` at runtime for metric alert detectors, where previously evaluate() returned an empty list harmlessly. Either keep a concrete stub implementation or register no handler until implemented.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Multi-group test builds expected occurrence with the wrong value

For `group_2` the data packet value is 10, but the expected occurrence is built with `value=6`. The assertion only passes because the mock occurrence ignores `value`; if build_occurrence_and_event_data ever incorporates the value the test would silently be asserting the wrong thing. Pass 10 to keep the expectation faithful.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

false_positives.candidate:
PriorityLevel(new_status) can raise ValueError

`PriorityLevel(new_status)` casts a DetectorPriorityLevel into the unrelated PriorityLevel enum. Any DetectorPriorityLevel value that doesn't have a numerically identical PriorityLevel member will raise ValueError during evaluation, crashing detector processing. The conversion should go through an explicit mapping with a safe fallback rather than relying on the two enums' numeric values staying in sync.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
get_monitor_environment_context computes `config` copy but returns the raw config

Lines 160-162 copy the monitor config and replace `schedule_type` with its display value, but the returned dict at line 168 uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the modified `config`. The resulting occurrence context therefore reports the numeric schedule_type rather than the human-readable one, and the copy is dead code. (Carried over from the moved code, but easy to fix while relocating.)

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Removed public names from mark_failed without re-exports

`mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context` and `SimpleCheckIn` were all removed from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` and moved/renamed into new modules, with no backwards-compatible aliases. Any existing imports (e.g. tests patching `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence`, or code importing `SimpleCheckIn` from here) will fail at import time or silently stop patching the real code path. Either keep re-export aliases or update all call sites/tests in this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag name: 'shards' vs 'shard'

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged `shards=shard_tag` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `shard=shard_tag`. Inconsistent tag keys break dashboards/queries that group by one key. Pick one key name for all flusher metrics.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is never true for spawn processes, so unhealthy flushers are never killed

In `_ensure_processes_alive` the kill is now guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Processes here are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which produces `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances; `SpawnProcess` is a subclass of `BaseProcess`, not of `multiprocessing.Process` (= `context.Process`). So the isinstance check is False and `process.kill()` is never invoked. A hung (but still alive) flusher process will not be killed before `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement, leaking live processes that keep flushing the same shards concurrently — duplicate segment production and growing process count up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS. The same flaw makes `process.terminate()` in `join()` a no-op.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of loop leaving remaining processes unterminated

In `join`, when the deadline is exceeded the loop `break`s, so any processes after the current index are never waited on nor terminated. On shutdown/rebalance with multiple flusher processes, some child processes are left running (they are daemons, so they die with the parent, but during arroyo rebalances the parent keeps running) and may keep flushing shards that have been reassigned. Also `remaining_time` is computed and unused. Terminate all processes unconditionally before returning.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead method _create_process_for_shard

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is not called from anywhere after the refactor (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards`). Dead code that duplicates restart logic and will rot; remove it.

New test asserts only process counts, not shard distribution or flushing correctness

`test_flusher_processes_limit` checks `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and that the total shard count is 4, but never asserts that shards are evenly distributed (2 per process) nor that segments from all four shards actually get produced through the multiple processes. The core behaviour this PR introduces (parallel flushing across processes, restart handling) is untested.

Per-shard unhealthy metric increases cardinality and double-counts a single process failure

`spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` is now emitted once per shard owned by the failing process, with a `shard` tag. One process failure produces N increments, so the metric no longer counts failures and the `shard` tag adds cardinality proportional to total shards. Consider emitting once per process (e.g. tagged with process index or the joined shard tag).

num_processes becomes 0 when no shards are assigned, silently disabling the flusher

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` plus `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` yields 0 when `buffer.assigned_shards` is empty (possible when a consumer is assigned no partitions). No flusher processes are started and no health check ever fires, so the strategy silently never flushes; additionally `max_processes` passed as 0 from the CLI would behave as "one process per shard" rather than an error. Validate the input and handle the empty-shard case explicitly.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts nothing meaningful about offsets

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` ends with `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which is a tautology (both branches assert the same thing) and, more importantly, contradicts the test's stated intent that "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages" — the implementation does commit offsets after a failure (the worker completes the offset in `finally`). The assertion will pass even if commits are completely broken; it should assert the expected committed offset (102).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Kafka integration test drives StreamProcessor via private APIs and sleeps

`test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` calls `processor._run_once()` / `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo APIs that can change without notice) and busy-loops for a fixed 5 seconds, which makes the test both brittle against arroyo upgrades and slow/flaky under load. The `commits_made` assertions are also guarded by `if commits_made:` so they silently no-op if no commit was recorded.

Lock creation relies on CPython dict atomicity

`_get_partition_lock` does an unsynchronized `get` followed by `setdefault` on a plain dict. This happens to be safe only because of CPython's GIL making `setdefault` atomic; it is not guaranteed by the language and would break under a free-threaded build. Prefer a single module-level lock guarding lock creation, or a `defaultdict(threading.Lock)` created once under a lock.

OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition revocation

`OffsetTracker` lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool`, and there is no API to drop state for revoked partitions. After a rebalance, `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` still contain entries for partitions this consumer no longer owns, so the commit thread can emit commits for partitions owned by another member, and stale `last_committed` values for a re-assigned partition can suppress legitimate commits (the loop only commits offsets greater than `last_committed`, which may now be far ahead of the new fetch position).

Transaction name hardcodes 'monitors' prefix for remote subscriptions worker

The sentry transaction name is `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`, but this is generic remote-subscription/uptime code. Including `worker_id` also produces high-cardinality transaction names (one per queue). This will make the uptime consumer's traces show up under misleading `monitors.*` names.

Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim

The docstrings for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` and `FixedQueuePool` claim "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but the queues are created as unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. A slow `result_processor` therefore causes unbounded growth of queued `WorkItem`s (each holding the full Kafka `Message`), leading to OOM rather than backpressure, and the comment is misleading. Give the queues a maxsize and raise `MessageRejected` when full.

commit function invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ends up in arroyo's `Commit` callback and ultimately the Kafka consumer. Arroyo strategies are documented as being driven from the single processing thread; the underlying consumer and the processor's offset bookkeeping are not thread-safe. Concurrent `commit()` from this thread while the main loop polls/commits can corrupt offset state or raise from librdkafka, risking duplicate or lost processing.

queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were added in Python 3.13. On any earlier interpreter, `except queue.ShutDown` in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` raises `AttributeError` when an exception propagates, and `q.shutdown(...)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` raises `AttributeError` which is swallowed by the bare `except Exception`. The result is that workers block forever in `work_queue.get()` (the `self.shutdown` flag is only checked between items), so shutdown takes 5s per worker and in-flight work is abandoned. If 3.13 is a hard requirement it should be stated; otherwise use a sentinel item plus `get(timeout=...)`.

strategy.close() destroys the factory-shared queue pool, breaking rebalances

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but the `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared across every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo closes/recreates the strategy on every partition rebalance, so after the first revoke the pool's worker threads are dead and its queues are shut down, while `factory.queue_pool` is still non-None. The next `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` will happily build a strategy over the dead pool and every submitted message will be silently dropped (or raise on `put` into a shut-down queue), stalling the consumer until the process is restarted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not prove the permission cache is bypassed

The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but the permCache entry is set to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}, i.e. a deny, so the assertion assert.False(resp.Allowed) would pass even if the denial cache were not consulted at all. Set the value to true (an allow) so the test actually verifies that the denial cache short-circuits before the permission cache.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous and omits group/resource

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, user UID, action, name and parent folder with '_' separators. Since resource/folder UIDs may legally contain underscores, two different (name, parent) pairs can produce the identical key (e.g. name="a_b", parent="c" vs name="a", parent="b_c"), causing a denial cached for one resource to be returned for a different one. The key also does not include group/resource, so two different group/resource pairs that map to the same action string would share denial entries. The consequence is incorrect (false) denials for up to the cache TTL. Include a non-ambiguous separator/encoding (e.g. length-prefixed or escaped segments) and the group/resource in the key.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Error from getCachedIdentityPermissions silently swallowed

In Check, the error from getCachedIdentityPermissions is only compared against nil; real errors (e.g. GetUserIdentifiers DB failure or 'unsupported identity type') are indistinguishable from cache.ErrNotFound and are neither logged nor traced. This hides genuine failures and makes debugging cache/identity-store problems hard. Distinguish cache.ErrNotFound from other errors and log/return the latter.

permissionCacheUsage metric counted twice for a single Check

When cached permissions are found but do not grant access, the code increments permissionCacheUsage with label "false" at line 137 after having consulted the cache successfully; conversely a denial-cache hit at line 118 increments "true" and then returns. The 'false' bucket therefore counts cache hits that simply didn't grant permission, so the cache hit-rate metric no longer reflects actual cache hits and will look much worse than reality.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing React `key` on GrafanaRuleListItem in list rendering

In the `rules.map(...)` loop the `grafana` branch renders `<GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} .../>` without passing `key={key}`, while all other branches do. React will emit a key warning and, more importantly, lose element identity across incremental page loads of the infinite-scroll list, which can cause incorrect re-use/re-ordering of rule rows and lost component state. Pass `key={key}` as before.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is a no-op when only a Prometheus rule is provided

`canSilence` in AlertRuleMenu can now be satisfied via the Grafana prom-rule abilities, so the "Silence notifications" item is rendered in the new list view. Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but the drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, i.e. when a ruler rule exists. In the list view `rule` is undefined, so the user clicks Silence and nothing happens.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and Pause actions silently disappear in the new rule list view

Abilities are now also derived from `promRule` (`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`), so `canDelete`/`canPause` can be true when only a Prometheus rule is available. However the Delete menu item is still gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` and the Pause item on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. Since the list view no longer fetches ruler rules (GrafanaRuleListItem passes only `promRule`), Delete and Pause are never rendered there — a functional regression versus the previous GrafanaRuleLoader which supplied `rulerRule`. Either keep fetching the ruler rule for these actions or implement prom-rule-based variants.

Federated rule-group check dropped, allowing edit/delete of federated rules

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`; it now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, where `isFederated` is hard-coded to `false`. Federated (Mimir cross-tenant) rule groups were intentionally treated as immutable; with this change Update/Delete/Pause abilities are reported as supported for them, exposing edit/delete UI for rules that cannot be modified.

Removed coverage for Creating/Deleting rule operation states without replacement

The tests for "ruler-only rule shows Creating state", "prom-only rule shows Deleting state" and the whole `matchRules` suite were deleted. `GrafanaRuleListItem` still accepts an `operation` prop and `RuleOperation.Creating/Deleting` still exist, but nothing now exercises or verifies the eventual-consistency UI behaviour, so regressions there will go unnoticed.

Rule-type check placed in the 'allowed' slot of the Silence ability

`[AlertRuleAction.Silence]: [silenceSupported, canSilenceInFolder && isAlertingRule]` puts `isAlertingRule` (a support condition, not a permission) into the 'allowed' position. Callers that only inspect `supported` (e.g. to decide whether to render a disabled control) will treat recording rules as silenceable. Move `isAlertingRule` into the supported flag to match the ruler-based implementation semantics.

Stale comment/variable name after removing ruler prefetch

The ruler `prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup')` dispatch was removed, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules..." and the variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`. This is misleading for future readers since no ruler data is preloaded anymore.

View link no longer carries returnTo parameter

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` built the href with `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component drops `returnTo`, so navigating back from the rule detail view loses the user's previous list position/filters.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Assertion on applyTemplateVariables call count encodes the double-interpolation behaviour

The test now asserts `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` for a single target. This number is an artifact of interpolation being re-applied inside runSplitQuery for each shard sub-request; it locks in the duplicate-interpolation behaviour and will break on any unrelated change to the number of shard groups, rather than testing that interpolation happens once up front.

Pre-interpolation can defeat the $__range split guard

querySupportsSplitting() relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to avoid splitting queries that use $__range (because the backend interpolates it per split range). Now that targets are interpolated before this check, any `$__range`/`$__range_ms`/`$__range_s` occurrence that templateSrv resolves on the frontend will already be substituted, so the guard no longer matches and the query gets split anyway — reintroducing the exact incorrect-range bug the guard was added for. The range check should run against the original, un-interpolated expression (or the guard moved before interpolation).

Queries are now interpolated twice in the shard-splitting path

runShardSplitQuery() now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on every target, and the resulting sub-requests are handed to runSplitQuery() (querySplitting.ts:296-299), which was changed in the same PR to also call applyTemplateVariables() on request.targets. Every shard sub-query therefore gets interpolated a second time (the new shard test even asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times for a single target). Double interpolation re-runs variable/ad-hoc-filter/regex-escape logic over already substituted text: variable values that themselves contain `$`/`{{}}` syntax get expanded again, and ad-hoc filters (request.filters) can be appended twice to the selector, producing wrong queries. Interpolation should happen in exactly one place.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID may be dropped from plugin request logs

The explicit `traceID` log param (previously added via tracing.TraceIDFromContext) was removed and replaced by m.logger.FromContext(ctx). This only preserves the traceID field if the infra logger's FromContext injects it and the span is recording; otherwise plugin egress logs lose correlation with traces, breaking existing log queries/dashboards that filter on traceID.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, discarding recorded logs

TestLogger.FromContext (and New) returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of the receiver. Since LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), any test using log.TestLogger to assert on InfoLogs/ErrorLogs counts and messages will observe zero calls, because the log is recorded on a throwaway instance. This silently makes existing/future logger-middleware assertions vacuous. Return the same instance (or one sharing the same Logs state).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Contextual logger not applied to stream endpoints

SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream pass the context through unchanged, so logs emitted downstream for streaming requests get no pluginId/dsUID/endpoint attributes. Since this middleware's sole purpose is enriching the context, adding instrumentContext for these three endpoints would make logging consistent across all client methods.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert device limit check is not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice reads CountDevices and then performs the insert in a separate session. Under concurrent anonymous requests several goroutines can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the configured device_limit can be exceeded by an arbitrary amount. Enforcement needs to be done inside a transaction (or via a conditional insert) if the limit is meant to be a hard cap.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path, adding DB round-trips per request

TagDevice was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own timeout; it is now called inline in Authenticate. Every anonymous authentication that misses the local cache now blocks on a COUNT query plus an upsert against anon_device, and any DB slowness/latency now directly affects anonymous request latency and can fail authentication (errors other than ErrDeviceLimitReached are only logged, but the latency remains). Worth confirming this is intended and bounding it (context timeout).

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is populated before the device is persisted, allowing the device limit to be bypassed

In tagDeviceUI the cache key is set with a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) before CreateOrUpdateDevice is called. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice/updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and the request is rejected, but the key stays in the local cache for ~29 minutes. On the next request with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id, tagDeviceUI returns nil early (cache hit) and the anonymous user is authenticated without ever being recorded, effectively bypassing the new limit for the whole cache TTL. The cache entry should only be stored after a successful store call.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rowsAffected == 0 is wrongly reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached for known devices on MySQL

updateDevice maps rowsAffected == 0 to ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, an UPDATE that matches a row but changes no column values reports 0 affected rows (CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS not set), so an existing, within-expiry device whose client_ip/user_agent/updated_at are unchanged (same second precision) will be treated as over the limit and the user will be denied access. Use rows-matched semantics or an explicit existence check instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
ErrDeviceLimitReached surfaces as a generic 500 to clients

ErrDeviceLimitReached is created with fmt.Errorf and returned verbatim from Authenticate. The authn layer has no mapping for it, so a user blocked by the device limit gets an opaque internal error rather than a meaningful status/message (e.g. 429/403 with explanation). Define it with errutil so the API returns an actionable response.

New auth.anonymous device_limit option is undocumented

cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from [auth.anonymous] device_limit but the option is not added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the configuration docs. Operators have no discoverable way to learn about the setting or its default (0 = unlimited).

anonymousDeviceLimit initialized to undefined infers type `undefined`

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` without an explicit annotation gives the property the type `undefined`, while the backend always sends a number (0 when unset) via merge(). Consumers that read it as a number will fail type checking, and the declared `number | undefined` in GrafanaConfig never actually becomes undefined. Annotate as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping full ID lists

r.log.Error(...) is used in CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) for purely informational messages, including the entire slice of IDs being deleted. On a busy instance with large batch sizes (e.g. 32767 IDs per batch) this will spam error-level logs with huge messages every cleanup cycle, trigger alerting on error logs, and is pure debug leftover. These should be Debug level (or removed), and the ID list should not be logged.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The background cleanup ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. The clean() routine itself has a 9-minute timeout, so runs can now overlap/queue up, and all cleanup jobs (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, query history) will execute 10x more often, increasing DB load significantly. This looks like leftover debugging from reproducing the deadlock and is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic fetch-then-delete can loop extra times and miscount

fetchIDs and deleteByIDs run in separate sessions, so rows found by the SELECT may already be gone when the DELETE runs. untilDoneOrCancelled only stops when affected==0, so in a concurrent scenario a batch that selects N ids but deletes 0 terminates the loop early (under-delete, as documented), but a batch that selects ids and deletes a subset keeps looping; combined with the MaxCount offset query this can repeatedly re-read the same rows. Consider terminating on len(ids)==0 rather than affected==0 so the loop semantics match the actual work remaining.

SQLite parameter-limit workaround keyed on batch size instead of actual ID count

deleteByIDs decides between inlined literals and bound parameters based on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999, not len(ids). The condition is also tied to GetDBType()==SQLite only. If any other code path (or a future caller) passes more IDs than the configured batch size, or if the configured batch size is unset/zero while a large slice is passed, the parameterized branch will be used with >999 placeholders and SQLite will fail with "too many SQL variables". Base the decision on len(ids) instead, and chunk the deletes so the statement is always within the driver limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses the base logger rather than `log`, so downstream code reading the logger from the context loses the name/kind/method values that were just attached. Every other method in the file passes `log`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection goroutine records legacy call as storage duration

Inside the async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine the result is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` with `startLegacy`. This attributes legacy latency/errors to the storage metric; it should be `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection failures will therefore never show up in the legacy error metric.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object name used as metric label in Delete success path

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Since names are unbounded (one per resource), this creates an unbounded number of Prometheus label values, causing cardinality explosion / memory growth in the metrics registry, and it also breaks comparability with the other recorded durations.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be cancelled

All four goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) derive their timeout context from the incoming request `ctx`. As soon as the HTTP handler returns (which happens immediately, since the goroutine is fired and the response is returned), the apiserver cancels the request context, which cancels the derived child context. The legacy write will then frequently fail with `context canceled` instead of running for its intended 10s budget, silently losing the legacy copy of the data. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) before applying the timeout.

Duplicate go.work.sum entry added

`github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` is added at line 408 while the identical line already exists a few lines above. These go.work.sum additions look like unrelated/accidental churn for a dual-writer change and should be dropped or regenerated.

Legacy Create is given the pre-create object which storage may have mutated

The goroutine passes the original `obj` to `d.Legacy.Create`. `d.Storage.Create` may have mutated `obj` in place (resourceVersion, UID, generated name) or the legacy store may generate a different name/UID, so the two stores can diverge in identity — exactly what mode 3's background legacy write is meant to prevent. Consider passing the returned `created` object (as mode 2's update path did with `updateWrapper`).

Mode 3 tests race with the async legacy goroutine and never assert it ran

The implementation now performs the legacy write in a goroutine, but the tests return as soon as the synchronous call completes. The same `*mock.Mock` is shared between the legacy and storage mocks, so the goroutine calls `m.Called(...)` concurrently with (or after) the test's assertions — a data race that `-race` will flag, and possibly a call into a `t` that has already finished. Additionally no test asserts that the legacy store was actually written to (e.g. via `mock.AssertExpectations` after waiting), so the core behaviour of mode 3 is untested. The tests need synchronization (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup signalled from the legacy mock) before asserting.

Storage failure recorded as legacy duration in Create and Update

On the storage error path of Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. The failing call was to unified storage, so this inflates the legacy error/duration metric and leaves storage failures unrecorded, making the mode-3 dashboards misleading.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock

After the read-lock fast path fails, the function takes the write lock but never re-reads entryPointAssetsCache. If N requests arrive concurrently on a cold cache, each one in turn will re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json (or hit the CDN) while serialized on the mutex, instead of the first filling the cache and the rest returning it. Re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache != nil` (for non-Dev env) right after Lock() avoids the redundant I/O and the resulting latency spike at startup.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Failed load overwrites a previously valid cached value with nil

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, including when readWebAssetsFromFile/CDN returned an error and result is nil. A single transient failure (e.g. file temporarily unreadable, CDN error) wipes an already-good cached value, so every subsequent call must reload and will return nil assets until a load succeeds. The assignment should be guarded by `if err == nil && result != nil`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions is dead logic that always returns false

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on both branches, so the feature-flag read has no effect and the function is a constant `false`. While the intent (hard-disabling SQL expressions) is achieved, the code is misleading: a reader/linter can't tell whether the flag is honoured, and a future edit to one branch could silently re-enable the vulnerable path. Replace with an explicit `return false` plus a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, or remove the helper and return the error directly.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy (non-reader) SQL expression path is not blocked, only stubbed

`UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` still accept SQL expression nodes; the feature-flag gate was only added in `reader.go` (ReadQuery). On the legacy query path, `sql.TablesList` now fails inside `NewSQLCommand`, returning a generic 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest, and `Execute` would return an opaque 'not implemented' as a query error. This makes the disable behaviour inconsistent and the failure mode confusing; the legacy path should explicitly reject SQL expressions with the same clear message.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading

Users enabling the still-present `sqlExpressions` feature toggle will get 'sqlExpressions is not implemented', which suggests a missing feature rather than a deliberately disabled one. Since the toggle remains documented, the message should state that SQL expressions are currently disabled, so operators don't file bugs or assume a build problem.

No test asserting SQL expressions are disabled

This PR disables a security-sensitive feature purely by stubbing out the DB implementation and adding an always-false flag check, but no test asserts that a QueryTypeSQL query is rejected. Without such a test, a future refactor (e.g. reintroducing an engine or 'fixing' enableSqlExpressions) can silently re-enable the RCE/LFI path. Add a unit test for ReadQuery with QueryTypeSQL expecting an error.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent BuildIndex for the same key can collide on the bleve directory and cache entry

BuildIndex no longer holds `cacheMu` for the whole function; the lock is only taken when writing the cache. Two concurrent calls for the same NamespacedResource (e.g. a watch event triggering `getOrCreateIndex` while startup indexing runs) will both call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same path, which fails (or corrupts) for file-backed indexes, and both will write to `b.cache[key]`, so one fully built index is silently discarded while readers may already hold it. Consider per-key locking / single-flight instead of no lock at all.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads the cache map without holding cacheMu

`TotalDocs` iterates `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu` (even read lock). Previously writes to the map happened while BuildIndex held the exclusive lock for its entire duration; now writes are short but can occur from watch-event-driven builds at any time. `init()` in search.go now calls `s.search.TotalDocs()` while such builds can be in flight, so a concurrent map read/write panic is possible. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in TotalDocs.

false_positives.candidate:
Context/goroutine leak when Init fails in NewResourceServer

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` and returns `nil, err` on failure, but the `cancel` from `context.WithCancel` created a few lines above is never called on this path. The derived context stays alive, and any goroutines already started by `s.search.init` (the watch-event consumer goroutine started before the failure point) are never stopped. Add `defer`/explicit `cancel()` before returning the error.

Data race on shared `err` variable in index-build errgroup

In `searchSupport.init`, each `group.Go` closure assigns to the function-scoped `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and `totalBatchesIndexed++` is incremented without synchronization. With `initWorkers > 1` these run concurrently, producing a genuine data race: build errors can be lost or overwritten (and `group.Wait()`'s result can be confused with a stale value), and the counter can be wrong. This matters more now that the coarse lock in `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` was removed, so the goroutines actually run in parallel. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic counter.

Stop() no longer prevents further request handling

`Stop()` sets `s.initErr = "service is stopping"/"service is stopped"` as the mechanism to reject requests, but all the `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil` guards were removed from Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/Blob handlers. After `Stop()` those handlers will keep serving requests against a cancelled background context and a stopped backend, instead of returning an error. Either re-add a lightweight 'is running' check to the handlers or drop the now-dead initErr mutation in Stop.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers removal of a provider named literally "alias"

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` uses the literal string "alias" instead of the actual alias ("idp-alias-" + i / "idp-alias-20"). Consequently none of the 21 identity providers created by testCacheIDPForLogin are removed after the test (the cleanup targets a non-existent provider and will either no-op or throw), leaking state into other tests in the class/realm and making counts in subsequent tests flaky. Same mistake appears at lines 303 and 425.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin cache is not invalidated on organization changes

Unlike getByOrganization(), which checks `isInvalid(orgId)`, getForLogin() only checks the login cache key. If an organization is disabled, removed, or its IDP links change outside IdentityProviderStorageProvider.update() (e.g. OrganizationProvider operations that only invalidate the organization entry), the cached ID sets for ORG_ONLY/ALL remain stale. The PR compensates only in OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean by re-checking isEnabled() on the wrapped model; other consumers of getForLogin() get IDPs of disabled/removed organizations. Consider also checking isInvalid(organizationId) and registering login invalidation on organization updates/removal.

getLoginPredicate semantics changed for all callers

getLoginPredicate() now additionally requires that org-linked IDPs have `organization.broker.public=true`. This public static predicate is used by callers outside the new invalidation logic (e.g. identity provider beans/filters); any caller that previously accepted org-linked, non-public IDPs will now silently drop them. This behavioural change is not documented in the enum's javadoc and could change which brokers are shown/accepted in flows unrelated to the login page.

remove() now always performs a DB lookup by alias

`idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` is now executed unconditionally at the start of remove(), even when the alias is present in the cache (previously the DB lookup only happened on the invalidated path). This adds an extra query to every IDP removal. The cached CachedIdentityProvider could be reused to build the model needed for registerIDPLoginInvalidation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated provider

The method returns the provider of the default KeyStore type (e.g. SUN), which is not a BouncyCastle provider. Code paths such as BouncyIntegration/Provider-name based `getInstance(alg, provider)` lookups will silently use a provider that does not implement the expected algorithms, producing confusing NoSuchAlgorithmException errors far from the cause. Returning null or throwing UnsupportedOperationException (consistent with the other unimplemented methods) would be clearer.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: two ASN1Encoder instances created and discarded

Lines 114-115 create `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` / `...write(sBigInteger)` and discard the results; the actual DER sequence is built again on lines 117-121. These two statements have no effect and should be removed to avoid confusing readers into thinking state is accumulated.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added as an abstract method to the public `CryptoProvider` interface. Any third-party or out-of-tree implementation (e.g. custom crypto providers shipped by adapters or downstream projects) will fail to compile and will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime after upgrade. Since a sensible fallback exists, this should be a `default int order() { return 100; }` (or similar) to preserve binary/source compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Ambiguous provider selection when orders are equal is now silent

Previously multiple CryptoProviders on the classpath caused an IllegalStateException. Now providers are sorted by order and the first is chosen; if two providers share the same order (all in-tree providers use 200, e.g. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider), the selection depends on ServiceLoader iteration order and is effectively non-deterministic, with only a debug log. A conflicting FIPS/non-FIPS selection would be a silent, hard-to-diagnose misconfiguration; consider logging a warning (or failing) when the top two providers have equal order.

Indefinite length (-1) leads to NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException

`readLength()` returns -1 for the indefinite-length encoding (0x80). In `readInteger()` (line 71-72) and `readNext()` that value is passed straight to `read(int length)`, which does `new byte[length]` and will throw an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException on malformed/attacker-supplied DER instead of the declared IOException. Callers parsing untrusted signatures (asn1derToConcatenatedRS) would get an unexpected runtime exception. Reject indefinite length explicitly with an IOException.

Test uses a default (P-256) EC key for ES384/ES512 cases

`KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` uses the JDK default curve (typically secp256r1) for all three tests, so testES384/testES512 never exercise real P-384/P-521 signatures; r/s are just zero-padded to the larger length. Initialize the generator with the matching `ECGenParameterSpec` per algorithm so the conversion is validated for real ES384/ES512 signature sizes.

logger.debugf called with a dynamically built string as format

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a runtime-constructed string as the format argument with no parameters. If any class name (or future content) contains a `%` sequence, formatting will fail/produce garbage. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE when the 'Clients' resource-type resource is missing

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String) when no per-client resource exists, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource(...), which can return null (it returns null when the realm does not support the authorization schema, when the resource type is unknown, or when the resource was never created/was deleted). The returned value is immediately passed to policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) and later to new ResourcePermission(resource, resource.getScopes(), server), causing a NullPointerException (HTTP 500) instead of a clean 403. A null check returning false is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: unused getEvaluationContext and unused imports/constants

getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) is private and never referenced (canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException), as are the logger field, the static TOKEN_EXCHANGE import and the Scope/ClientModelIdentity/DefaultEvaluationContext imports. Dead code copied from V1 misleads readers into thinking token-exchange evaluation is wired up; it should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

false_positives.candidate:
Listener throws UnsupportedOperationException when both FGAP v1 and v2 are enabled

registerListener now only runs when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (v1) is enabled, but management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. If both features are enabled simultaneously, removing a client triggers clients().setPermissionsEnabled(...) on ClientPermissionsV2, which throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"), breaking client/role/group deletion. The guard should also exclude the case where v2 is active (or the v1 implementation should be used explicitly here).

getResourceName not implemented for the new Clients resource type

getResourceName handles only USERS: for a policy with resourceType 'Clients' it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is not set for resources created by getOrCreateResource (resources are created with name=client UUID and no display name). As a result admin/UI consumers get null instead of the client's clientId, or 'Clients' instead of a readable 'All clients' label. Add a Clients branch resolving the client by id.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code semantics swapped: 4 changes meaning from 'recreate needed' to 'feature disabled'

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE moved from 4 to 3 and 4 is now reused for FEATURE_DISABLED. Any existing automation/script (or operator logic) that treats exit code 4 as "recreate upgrade required" will now silently interpret a feature-disabled run (where no compatibility check happened at all) as "recreate required", and will not recognize the new code 3. Since both meanings are mutually inconsistent, this is a breaking contract change that should be called out in release/upgrade notes, and ideally the feature-disabled code should be a fresh value rather than the previously used 4.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
No assertion on exit code for feature-disabled path, and check subcommand not covered

testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the error message for the `metadata` subcommand. The newly introduced exit code (CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED = 4) is the documented contract for scripting, but no test verifies it; likewise the `check` subcommand's feature-disabled behaviour is untested. A regression in the exit code (e.g. the recent 3/4 renumbering) would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage on all groups to holders of only the VIEW scope

The no-arg `canManage()` evaluates `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, i.e. it returns true if the admin only has the `view` scope on the Groups resource type. `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup()` calls `auth.groups().requireManage()`, so an admin granted only all-groups `view` can create top-level groups (and any other check routed through `canManage()`), which is a privilege escalation. It should only check `MANAGE`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs instead of group IDs, and permission lookup by resource id fails

In the `findByType` callback, `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` is called, but `hasPermission` resolves the resource via `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` and the Groups resources are named by the *group id* (see `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup`, which returns `group.getId()` as the resource name). Passing the authz resource UUID therefore never matches, so the method silently falls back to the all-groups resource evaluation and the per-group `view-members`/`manage-members` grants are ignored. Likewise the IDs added to `granted` are authz resource IDs, but the returned set is used as `UserModel.GROUPS` in `UsersResource.searchForUser`/`getUsersCount` and `BruteForceUsersResource`, where group IDs are expected, so user searches/counts scoped by group membership return wrong results. Use `groupResource.getName()` in both places.

false_positives.candidate:
Javadoc for requireManageMembers references the wrong method

The Javadoc above `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` states it throws if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false; it actually delegates to `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`. The duplicated doc is misleading for implementors of the interface.

Possible NullPointerException when the Groups resource-type resource is absent

`AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource(...)` returns null when admin permissions are not enabled for the resource server, when the resource type is unknown, or when the 'Groups' resource is missing from the store. The returned value is used immediately in `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and `resource.getScopes()` without a null check, causing an NPE instead of a clean deny. Add a null guard returning false.

getResourceName does not resolve names for the new Groups resource type

`getResourceName` only special-cases `USERS`; for the newly added `GROUPS` resource type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`. Since group resources are stored with the raw group id as name and no display name, the admin UI/REST representation of a group-scoped permission will show an empty/raw id instead of the group path or name. Add a Groups branch resolving the group (and 'All groups' for the type resource).

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian translation replaced with Italian text

`loginTotpStep1` was replaced with `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:` which is Italian, not Lithuanian. Lithuanian users will see an Italian sentence. The same wrong text was introduced in themes/src/main/resources-community/theme/base/account/messages/messages_lt.properties (totpStep1).

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Simplified-Chinese bundle given Traditional Chinese text

`totpStep1` was set to `在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：`, which is Traditional Chinese (zh_TW) wording/characters, in the zh_CN (Simplified) bundle. Should use Simplified characters, e.g. `在您的手机上安装以下应用程序之一：`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Common-prefix/suffix trimming can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException

The two loops computing `start` and `end` are independent, so `start + end` can exceed the string length when the differing part is a repetition of surrounding characters (e.g. value="aa", sanitized="aaa" yields start=2, end=2). The subsequent `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` then gets end index < begin index and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException, crashing the build with an opaque error instead of reporting the illegal HTML. Clamp `end` to `min(end, length - start)` for both strings.

Missing English reference bundle aborts verification with RuntimeException

`verifySafeHtml()` derives the English file path by string replacement and throws an unchecked RuntimeException if it cannot be opened. Any bundle whose English counterpart does not exist at the derived path (community-only message directories, bundles without a locale suffix, or paths where the `resources-community`→`resources` substitution does not yield a real file) will fail the build with a raw RuntimeException instead of a MojoExecutionException/skippable warning. Handle the missing-file case explicitly (skip or report a message).

No positive test that a clean bundle yields no findings

All new tests assert that a violation is reported; none asserts the opposite (e.g. verifying `noHtml_en.properties` or a file with allowed `<b>`/anchor identical to English returns an empty message list). Without such a test, a regression that makes the sanitizer report false positives for legitimate messages (a likely outcome given the unescaping/`<!-- -->` hacks) would go undetected.

i18next message converted to Java MessageFormat/choice syntax

The account-ui (and admin-ui) message bundles are consumed by the React apps through i18next, which interpolates `{{0}}`-style placeholders and has no support for Java MessageFormat `{0}` or `{2,choice,...}`. Changing `error-invalid-multivalued-size` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.` means the end user will see the literal text `{0}`, `{1}` and `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` instead of substituted values. The same applies to js/apps/admin-ui/.../messages_en.properties:3138. Only the server-side themes/ bundles (Freemarker/MessageFormat) can use the choice syntax.

santizeAnchors removes the wrong anchor occurrence and reports without file context

Inside the loop, `value.replaceFirst(...)` always strips the *first* occurrence of the English anchor tag in the (already modified) value, while `matcher` still iterates the original string. With more than one identical anchor tag per message the positions get out of sync, so a mismatched/injected anchor can be silently removed (false negative) or a valid one flagged. Also the message added at line 157 contains neither the key nor the file name, making the failure hard to locate; all other messages include them.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null check for rawTokenId checks grantType instead

`Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` duplicates the previous grantType check, so a null `rawTokenId` is never rejected. A null raw token id then silently produces a token id like "onrtac:null" during encoding instead of failing fast.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted condition and wrong substring offsets

The matcher extracts the grant shortcut with `items[0].substring(3, 5)`, but the encoded prefix is sessionType(2)+tokenType(2)+grantType(2), so the grant shortcut lives at indices 4..6; indices 3..5 straddle the token-type and grant-type shortcuts. In addition the comparison is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` fails the match when the shortcut *does* equal the expected value. As written the matcher accepts any token id whose prefix differs from the expectation and rejects correct ones, so all the new assertions on Details.TOKEN_ID verify nothing (or the wrong thing). Should be `substring(4, 6)` and `if (!...equals(...)) return false;`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Lazy shortcut registration bypasses duplicate-shortcut validation

`getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut` add entries to both maps at runtime without checking whether the shortcut is already mapped to a different grant type (the only duplicate validation happens once in postInit). A newly deployed grant with a colliding shortcut will silently overwrite `grantsByShortcuts`, so token ids encoded with that shortcut will decode to the wrong grant type.

Removal of public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context) breaks SPI compatibility

The copy constructor `public Context(Context context)` was deleted from the public SPI class `OAuth2GrantType.Context` in server-spi-private. Any custom grant-type provider (or internal code built against previous versions) using it will no longer compile/link. false_positives.candidate:
strategy.close() destroys the factory-shared queue pool, breaking rebalances

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but the `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared across every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo closes/recreates the strategy on every partition rebalance, so after the first revoke the pool's worker threads are dead and its queues are shut down, while `factory.queue_pool` is still non-None. The next `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` will happily build a strategy over the dead pool and every submitted message will be silently dropped (or raise on `put` into a shut-down queue), stalling the consumer until the process is restarted.

commit function invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ends up in arroyo's `Commit` callback and ultimately the Kafka consumer. Arroyo strategies are documented as being driven from the single processing thread; the underlying consumer and the processor's offset bookkeeping are not thread-safe. Concurrent `commit()` from this thread while the main loop polls/commits can corrupt offset state or raise from librdkafka, risking duplicate or lost processing.

OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition revocation

`OffsetTracker` lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool`, and there is no API to drop state for revoked partitions. After a rebalance, `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` still contain entries for partitions this consumer no longer owns, so the commit thread can emit commits for partitions owned by another member, and stale `last_committed` values for a re-assigned partition can suppress legitimate commits (the loop only commits offsets greater than `last_committed`, which may now be far ahead of the new fetch position).

queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were added in Python 3.13. On any earlier interpreter, `except queue.ShutDown` in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` raises `AttributeError` when an exception propagates, and `q.shutdown(...)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` raises `AttributeError` which is swallowed by the bare `except Exception`. The result is that workers block forever in `work_queue.get()` (the `self.shutdown` flag is only checked between items), so shutdown takes 5s per worker and in-flight work is abandoned. If 3.13 is a hard requirement it should be stated; otherwise use a sentinel item plus `get(timeout=...)`.

Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim

The docstrings for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` and `FixedQueuePool` claim "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but the queues are created as unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. A slow `result_processor` therefore causes unbounded growth of queued `WorkItem`s (each holding the full Kafka `Message`), leading to OOM rather than backpressure, and the comment is misleading. Give the queues a maxsize and raise `MessageRejected` when full.

Lock creation relies on CPython dict atomicity

`_get_partition_lock` does an unsynchronized `get` followed by `setdefault` on a plain dict. This happens to be safe only because of CPython's GIL making `setdefault` atomic; it is not guaranteed by the language and would break under a free-threaded build. Prefer a single module-level lock guarding lock creation, or a `defaultdict(threading.Lock)` created once under a lock.

Transaction name hardcodes 'monitors' prefix for remote subscriptions worker

The sentry transaction name is `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`, but this is generic remote-subscription/uptime code. Including `worker_id` also produces high-cardinality transaction names (one per queue). This will make the uptime consumer's traces show up under misleading `monitors.*` names.

Kafka integration test drives StreamProcessor via private APIs and sleeps

`test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` calls `processor._run_once()` / `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo APIs that can change without notice) and busy-loops for a fixed 5 seconds, which makes the test both brittle against arroyo upgrades and slow/flaky under load. The `commits_made` assertions are also guarded by `if commits_made:` so they silently no-op if no commit was recorded.
