false_positives.candidate:
Hardcoded 1000-span cap silently drops spans and ignores max_segment_spans config

Eviction uses a literal `1000` instead of the configurable `max_segment_spans` (1001 in SpansBuffer), and `zpopmin` silently discards the oldest spans with no metric or log. The previous behavior (dropping the whole oversized segment with `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` + error log) was observable; now data loss is invisible. Pass the limit in as an ARGV and emit a metric/return the number evicted.

span_count may be stale, causing over- or under-eviction

`span_count` is set from the result of `zunionstore` calls, but when both unions run the second overwrites the first, and in either case the count reflects the set state before the Python-side `zadd` of new payloads in this batch happens relative to other pipeline commands. Only when `span_count == 0` is `zcard` consulted. If a union ran, the count can be lower than the actual cardinality, so a segment can exceed the cap, or (if a union inflated the count) spans can be evicted unnecessarily. Always read `zcard set_key` right before the cap check.

Redirect-chain loop limit reduced 10000 -> 1000 without justification, and explanatory comment removed

The loop bound was lowered from 10000 to 1000 and the comment warning that chains deeper than the bound may not be joined correctly was deleted. Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects will now silently fail to merge, producing split segments. This is unrelated to the eviction change; if intentional it needs a metric/alert and a comment, otherwise restore 10000.

max_segment_spans is now dead config while enforcement moved to a Lua literal

`self.max_segment_spans` is still a constructor parameter but no longer used anywhere after the span-count check was removed from `_load_segment_data`; the limit is hardcoded as 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Operators tuning `max_segment_spans` will have no effect, and the two values (1001 vs 1000) disagree. Wire the parameter through to the script or remove it.

zadd keyed on payload: duplicate payloads collapse and score is overwritten

Switching from `sadd` to `zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise})` makes the payload the sorted-set member. Two spans with byte-identical payloads still collapse to one entry (same as the set), but now re-ingesting a span also rewrites its score, which changes its eviction priority. More importantly, eviction by `zpopmin` on `end_timestamp_precise` drops the *earliest-ending* spans — typically the root/parent spans of a segment — rather than the least useful ones, which can destroy segment structure. Worth documenting/justifying, and the module docstring (lines 39-44, 58) still describes these keys as "sets" with `sadd` semantics.

__reduce__ omits new/existing fields, so pickled buffers lose configuration

`__reduce__` only passes `assigned_shards`, the two timeouts and `redis_ttl`, dropping `segment_page_size`, `max_segment_bytes` and `max_segment_spans`. In multiprocessing mode the buffer is pickled to subprocesses, so any non-default values for those limits are silently reset to defaults in workers.

No test for the new eviction-during-insert behavior

The PR's stated purpose is eviction during insert, but tests only add the now-required `end_timestamp_precise` field. There is no test that inserts more than the cap into one segment and asserts which spans are retained/evicted, nor a test that the removed `max_segment_spans` read-path behavior is covered by the new Lua cap. Regressions in the eviction arithmetic (stale `span_count`, off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`) would go undetected.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new public paginator wired into a production endpoint but has no unit tests covering next/prev cursors, negative offsets, or the datetime key path. Given it duplicates ~60 lines of `BasePaginator.get_result` with subtle differences, untested divergence is likely.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

The surrounding `try/catch` can no longer catch failures (rejections happen after the catch block has been left), so errors become unhandled promise rejections instead of being logged, and the function proceeds to send the reschedule email (and returns) before the external events are actually deleted. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
import() invoked eagerly at module load defeats lazy loading

The object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")` etc. immediately when `packages/app-store/index.ts` is evaluated, so every app module is still loaded (and its side effects run) on first access to the app store. The only change versus static imports is that consumers must now `await`; there is no code-splitting or startup-time benefit. To actually defer loading, the values must be thunks (`applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and call sites must invoke them. Additionally, if any of these module evaluations rejects, the stored promise has no attached handler at creation time, producing an unhandled promise rejection that can crash the Node process even if no code ever reads that app.

getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in `calendar`, breaking other consumers

`getCalendar` is now async, so `getCalendarCredentials()` returns items whose `calendar` field is a `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`. Any other caller of `getCalendarCredentials` that uses `.calendar` directly (e.g. truthiness checks or method calls) will now silently treat a promise as a calendar object, and a rejected promise that is never awaited becomes an unhandled rejection. All consumers of this return shape need auditing/updating.

async callback in forEach: deletions not awaited and errors escape try/catch

The `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` callback returns a promise that nobody awaits, so the external calendar/video deletions run detached. The enclosing `try/catch` no longer captures their failures (they surface as unhandled rejections), and the email is sent and the function returns before deletion completes. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`.

requestReschedule deletions are fire-and-forget after making callback async

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` is not awaited, so calendar event deletion / meeting deletion now happen after the tRPC mutation has already responded. Failures become unhandled rejections with no logging, and in serverless environments the process may be frozen before the deletes complete, leaving orphaned calendar events. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`.

Recurring-booking calendar deletes pushed into apiDeletes after it is already awaited

In the recurring branch the callback passed to `forEach` is `async` and awaits `getCalendar(credential)` plus `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` before `apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent)`. Because `forEach` does not await, control returns immediately and `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line 652) runs with an `apiDeletes` array that is still empty for these entries. The recurring calendar deletions are therefore neither awaited nor error-handled; with the extra `await getCalendar` introduced here the race is now guaranteed rather than incidental. Collect the promises synchronously (e.g. `for ... of` with awaited getCalendar, pushing the unawaited deleteEvent promise).

Noisy log.info of CalendarService constructor on every calendar resolution

`log.info("calendarApp", calendarApp.lib.CalendarService)` runs on every call to `getCalendar`, which is on the hot path for availability, booking creation and cancellation. It serializes a class constructor into logs on every request, adding noise and overhead with no diagnostic value. This looks like leftover debug output and should be removed or downgraded to debug.

false_positives.candidate:
i18next message converted to Java MessageFormat/choice syntax

The account-ui (and admin-ui) message bundles are consumed by the React apps through i18next, which interpolates `{{0}}`-style placeholders and has no support for Java MessageFormat `{0}` or `{2,choice,...}`. Changing `error-invalid-multivalued-size` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.` means the end user will see the literal text `{0}`, `{1}` and `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` instead of substituted values. The same applies to js/apps/admin-ui/.../messages_en.properties:3138. Only the server-side themes/ bundles (Freemarker/MessageFormat) can use the choice syntax.

Common-prefix/suffix trimming can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException

The two loops computing `start` and `end` are independent, so `start + end` can exceed the string length when the differing part is a repetition of surrounding characters (e.g. value="aa", sanitized="aaa" yields start=2, end=2). The subsequent `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` then gets end index < begin index and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException, crashing the build with an opaque error instead of reporting the illegal HTML. Clamp `end` to `min(end, length - start)` for both strings.

Missing English reference bundle aborts verification with RuntimeException

`verifySafeHtml()` derives the English file path by string replacement and throws an unchecked RuntimeException if it cannot be opened. Any bundle whose English counterpart does not exist at the derived path (community-only message directories, bundles without a locale suffix, or paths where the `resources-community`→`resources` substitution does not yield a real file) will fail the build with a raw RuntimeException instead of a MojoExecutionException/skippable warning. Handle the missing-file case explicitly (skip or report a message).

santizeAnchors removes the wrong anchor occurrence and reports without file context

Inside the loop, `value.replaceFirst(...)` always strips the *first* occurrence of the English anchor tag in the (already modified) value, while `matcher` still iterates the original string. With more than one identical anchor tag per message the positions get out of sync, so a mismatched/injected anchor can be silently removed (false negative) or a valid one flagged. Also the message added at line 157 contains neither the key nor the file name, making the failure hard to locate; all other messages include them.

No positive test that a clean bundle yields no findings

All new tests assert that a violation is reported; none asserts the opposite (e.g. verifying `noHtml_en.properties` or a file with allowed `<b>`/anchor identical to English returns an empty message list). Without such a test, a regression that makes the sanitizer report false positives for legitimate messages (a likely outcome given the unescaping/`<!-- -->` hacks) would go undetected.

false_positives.candidate:
Federated recovery-code credential cannot track used codes, enabling code reuse

getCredential() now prefers the credential returned from the federated (user storage) credentials stream. Callers treat the result as a stateful RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel: RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean uses getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() to decide which code to ask for, and RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator calls removeStoredCredentialById() when all codes are used. For a federated credential there is no local row, so removeStoredCredentialById() is a no-op and the provider is never told that a code was consumed (e.g. BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials() always rebuilds the model from the raw list with no 'used' state). Consequence: the login form always requests code #0 and the same recovery code remains valid indefinitely — one-time codes become reusable, which defeats their security purpose.

Raw recovery codes are sent to user storage as plaintext JSON

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the full list of generated raw (unhashed) recovery codes into JSON and passes it as the UserCredentialModel value to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). Any user storage provider that supports the recovery-authn-codes type will receive and most likely persist the codes in clear text (as the test provider does). Local storage stores only salted hashes, so this is a significant weakening of the credential handling contract and should at least be documented/hashed before being handed off.

No feedback when neither user storage nor local creation succeeds / credential ID lost

createRecoveryCodesCredential returns void and swallows the outcome: if updateCredential() returns false, it unconditionally creates the credential locally, but it never reports whether the operation actually succeeded, and the caller (RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.processAction) calls reqActionContext.success() regardless. A failing provider (e.g. it accepted the type but discarded the value) would leave the user without usable recovery codes while the required action is marked complete.

getCredentials() dereferences possibly null MyUser

getMyUser(user) returns users.get(...) which can be null (other methods in this class explicitly null-check it, e.g. isConfiguredFor and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream). Accessing myUser.recoveryCodes immediately afterwards will throw NullPointerException for any user not present in the in-memory map (e.g. a stale cached federated user), breaking credential listing.

Test does not verify code consumption or exhaustion behaviour

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only logs in once with code #0. It does not assert that a used code is rejected on a subsequent login, nor that the prompted code number advances, which is exactly the behaviour that is broken for federated credentials. false_positives.candidate:
strategy.close() destroys the factory-shared queue pool, breaking rebalances

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but the `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared across every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo closes/recreates the strategy on every partition rebalance, so after the first revoke the pool's worker threads are dead and its queues are shut down, while `factory.queue_pool` is still non-None. The next `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` will happily build a strategy over the dead pool and every submitted message will be silently dropped (or raise on `put` into a shut-down queue), stalling the consumer until the process is restarted.

commit function invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ends up in arroyo's `Commit` callback and ultimately the Kafka consumer. Arroyo strategies are documented as being driven from the single processing thread; the underlying consumer and the processor's offset bookkeeping are not thread-safe. Concurrent `commit()` from this thread while the main loop polls/commits can corrupt offset state or raise from librdkafka, risking duplicate or lost processing.

OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition revocation

`OffsetTracker` lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool`, and there is no API to drop state for revoked partitions. After a rebalance, `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` still contain entries for partitions this consumer no longer owns, so the commit thread can emit commits for partitions owned by another member, and stale `last_committed` values for a re-assigned partition can suppress legitimate commits (the loop only commits offsets greater than `last_committed`, which may now be far ahead of the new fetch position).

queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were added in Python 3.13. On any earlier interpreter, `except queue.ShutDown` in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` raises `AttributeError` when an exception propagates, and `q.shutdown(...)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` raises `AttributeError` which is swallowed by the bare `except Exception`. The result is that workers block forever in `work_queue.get()` (the `self.shutdown` flag is only checked between items), so shutdown takes 5s per worker and in-flight work is abandoned. If 3.13 is a hard requirement it should be stated; otherwise use a sentinel item plus `get(timeout=...)`.

Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim

The docstrings for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` and `FixedQueuePool` claim "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but the queues are created as unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. A slow `result_processor` therefore causes unbounded growth of queued `WorkItem`s (each holding the full Kafka `Message`), leading to OOM rather than backpressure, and the comment is misleading. Give the queues a maxsize and raise `MessageRejected` when full.

Lock creation relies on CPython dict atomicity

`_get_partition_lock` does an unsynchronized `get` followed by `setdefault` on a plain dict. This happens to be safe only because of CPython's GIL making `setdefault` atomic; it is not guaranteed by the language and would break under a free-threaded build. Prefer a single module-level lock guarding lock creation, or a `defaultdict(threading.Lock)` created once under a lock.

The sentry transaction name is `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`, but this is generic remote-subscription/uptime code. Including `worker_id` also produces high-cardinality transaction names (one per queue). This will make the uptime consumer's traces show up under misleading `monitors.*` names.

`test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` calls `processor._run_once()` / `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo APIs that can change without notice) and busy-loops for a fixed 5 seconds, which makes the test both brittle against arroyo upgrades and slow/flaky under load. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock

After the read-lock fast path fails, the function takes the write lock but never re-reads entryPointAssetsCache. If N requests arrive concurrently on a cold cache, each one in turn will re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json (or hit the CDN) while serialized on the mutex, instead of the first filling the cache and the rest returning it. Re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache != nil` (for non-Dev env) right after Lock() avoids the redundant I/O and the resulting latency spike at startup.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock, which causes concurrent callers on a cold cache to redundantly populate it instead of using the cache filled by another goroutine.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Failed load overwrites a previously valid cached value with nil

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, including when readWebAssetsFromFile/CDN returned an error and result is nil. A single transient failure (e.g. file temporarily unreadable, CDN error) wipes an already-good cached value, so every subsequent call must reload and will return nil assets until a load succeeds. The assignment should be guarded by `if err == nil && result != nil`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the fetch result is assigned to entryPointAssetsCache unconditionally, so a failed fetch returning nil overwrites a previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

On a busy instance with large batch sizes (e.g. 32767 IDs per batch) this will spam error-level logs with huge messages every cleanup cycle, trigger alerting on error logs, and is pure debug leftover. true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

false_positives.candidate:

deleteByIDs decides between inlined literals and bound parameters based on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999, not len(ids). The condition is also tied to GetDBType()==SQLite only. If any other code path (or a future caller) passes more IDs than the configured batch size, or if the configured batch size is unset/zero while a large slice is passed, the parameterized branch will be used with >999 placeholders and SQLite will fail with "too many SQL variables". Base the decision on len(ids) instead, and chunk the deletes so the statement is always within the driver limit.

Non-atomic fetch-then-delete can loop extra times and miscount

fetchIDs and deleteByIDs run in separate sessions, so rows found by the SELECT may already be gone when the DELETE runs. untilDoneOrCancelled only stops when affected==0, so in a concurrent scenario a batch that selects N ids but deletes 0 terminates the loop early (under-delete, as documented), but a batch that selects ids and deletes a subset keeps looping; combined with the MaxCount offset query this can repeatedly re-read the same rows. Consider terminating on len(ids)==0 rather than affected==0 so the loop semantics match the actual work remaining.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object name used as metric label in Delete success path

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Since names are unbounded (one per resource), this creates an unbounded number of Prometheus label values, causing cardinality explosion / memory growth in the metrics registry, and it also breaks comparability with the other recorded durations.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same inconsistency: the Delete success path passes the object name instead of options.Kind to metrics recording, unlike other call sites. The additional cardinality concerns describe consequences of that same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be cancelled

All four goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) derive their timeout context from the incoming request `ctx`. As soon as the HTTP handler returns (which happens immediately, since the goroutine is fired and the response is returned), the apiserver cancels the request context, which cancels the derived child context. The legacy write will then frequently fail with `context canceled` instead of running for its intended 10s budget, silently losing the legacy copy of the data. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) before applying the timeout.

Storage failure recorded as legacy duration in Create and Update

On the storage error path of Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. The failing call was to unified storage, so this inflates the legacy error/duration metric and leaves storage failures unrecorded, making the mode-3 dashboards misleading.

DeleteCollection goroutine records legacy call as storage duration

Inside the async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine the result is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` with `startLegacy`. This attributes legacy latency/errors to the storage metric; it should be `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection failures will therefore never show up in the legacy error metric.

Mode 3 tests race with the async legacy goroutine and never assert it ran

The implementation now performs the legacy write in a goroutine, but the tests return as soon as the synchronous call completes. The same `*mock.Mock` is shared between the legacy and storage mocks, so the goroutine calls `m.Called(...)` concurrently with (or after) the test's assertions — a data race that `-race` will flag, and possibly a call into a `t` that has already finished. Additionally no test asserts that the legacy store was actually written to (e.g. via `mock.AssertExpectations` after waiting), so the core behaviour of mode 3 is untested. The tests need synchronization (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup signalled from the legacy mock) before asserting.

Legacy Create is given the pre-create object which storage may have mutated

The goroutine passes the original `obj` to `d.Legacy.Create`. `d.Storage.Create` may have mutated `obj` in place (resourceVersion, UID, generated name) or the legacy store may generate a different name/UID, so the two stores can diverge in identity — exactly what mode 3's background legacy write is meant to prevent. Consider passing the returned `created` object (as mode 2's update path did with `updateWrapper`).

Duplicate go.work.sum entry added

`github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` is added at line 408 while the identical line already exists a few lines above. These go.work.sum additions look like unrelated/accidental churn for a dual-writer change and should be dropped or regenerated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` built the href with `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component drops `returnTo`, so navigating back from the rule detail view loses the user's previous list position/filters.

The tests for "ruler-only rule shows Creating state", "prom-only rule shows Deleting state" and the whole `matchRules` suite were deleted. `GrafanaRuleListItem` still accepts an `operation` prop and `RuleOperation.Creating/Deleting` still exist, but nothing now exercises or verifies the eventual-consistency UI behaviour, so regressions there will go unnoticed.

`[AlertRuleAction.Silence]: [silenceSupported, canSilenceInFolder && isAlertingRule]` puts `isAlertingRule` (a support condition, not a permission) into the 'allowed' position. Callers that only inspect `supported` (e.g. to decide whether to render a disabled control) will treat recording rules as silenceable. The ruler `prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup')` dispatch was removed, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules..." and the variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`. This is misleading for future readers since no ruler data is preloaded anymore.

querySupportsSplitting() relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to avoid splitting queries that use $__range (because the backend interpolates it per split range). Now that targets are interpolated before this check, any `$__range`/`$__range_ms`/`$__range_s` occurrence that templateSrv resolves on the frontend will already be substituted, so the guard no longer matches and the query gets split anyway — reintroducing the exact incorrect-range bug the guard was added for. The test now asserts `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` for a single target. This number is an artifact of interpolation being re-applied inside runSplitQuery for each shard sub-request; it locks in the duplicate-interpolation behaviour and will break on any unrelated change to the number of shard groups, rather than testing that interpolation happens once up front.

Count-then-insert device limit check is not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice reads CountDevices and then performs the insert in a separate session. Under concurrent anonymous requests several goroutines can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the configured device_limit can be exceeded by an arbitrary amount. Enforcement needs to be done inside a transaction (or via a conditional insert) if the limit is meant to be a hard cap.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the limit. Both suggest transactional or atomic enforcement.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rowsAffected == 0 is wrongly reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached for known devices on MySQL

updateDevice maps rowsAffected == 0 to ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, an UPDATE that matches a row but changes no column values reports 0 affected rows (CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS not set), so an existing, within-expiry device whose client_ip/user_agent/updated_at are unchanged (same second precision) will be treated as over the limit and the user will be denied access. Use rows-matched semantics or an explicit existence check instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the incorrect mapping of rowsAffected == 0 to ErrDeviceLimitReached in updateDevice. The candidate describes an additional MySQL-specific cause of zero affected rows, but the underlying error-classification bug is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is populated before the device is persisted, allowing the device limit to be bypassed

In tagDeviceUI the cache key is set with a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) before CreateOrUpdateDevice is called. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice/updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and the request is rejected, but the key stays in the local cache for ~29 minutes. On the next request with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id, tagDeviceUI returns nil early (cache hit) and the anonymous user is authenticated without ever being recorded, effectively bypassing the new limit for the whole cache TTL. The cache entry should only be stored after a successful store call.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same premature cache insertion in tagDeviceUI: ErrDeviceLimitReached leaves the device ID cached, so subsequent requests bypass the device limit until the approximately 29-minute cache expiry.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path, adding DB round-trips per request

TagDevice was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own timeout; it is now called inline in Authenticate. Every anonymous authentication that misses the local cache now blocks on a COUNT query plus an upsert against anon_device, and any DB slowness/latency now directly affects anonymous request latency and can fail authentication (errors other than ErrDeviceLimitReached are only logged, but the latency remains). Worth confirming this is intended and bounding it (context timeout).

ErrDeviceLimitReached surfaces as a generic 500 to clients

ErrDeviceLimitReached is created with fmt.Errorf and returned verbatim from Authenticate. The authn layer has no mapping for it, so a user blocked by the device limit gets an opaque internal error rather than a meaningful status/message (e.g. 429/403 with explanation). Define it with errutil so the API returns an actionable response.

New auth.anonymous device_limit option is undocumented

cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from [auth.anonymous] device_limit but the option is not added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the configuration docs. Operators have no discoverable way to learn about the setting or its default (0 = unlimited).

anonymousDeviceLimit initialized to undefined infers type `undefined`

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` without an explicit annotation gives the property the type `undefined`, while the backend always sends a number (0 when unset) via merge(). Consumers that read it as a number will fail type checking, and the declared `number | undefined` in GrafanaConfig never actually becomes undefined. Annotate as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined`.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

ensure_loaded! initializes shared state outside the mutex

`@loaded_locales ||= []` and the subsequent `include?` check run outside LOAD_MUTEX, so two threads can concurrently assign different arrays to @loaded_locales, losing load bookkeeping and causing duplicate/missed locale loads. Move the initialization and check inside the synchronized block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify unsynchronized lazy initialization and concurrent access to @loaded_locales. The candidate specifically points out that initialization and the include? check occur outside the mutex, matching the golden thread-safety issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fallback locale keys may be strings, causing mismatched/unloaded locales

`[](locale)` returns `[locale, ...]` without normalizing `locale` to a symbol. I18n may pass strings (e.g. 'de'), so the chain can contain a String while `ensure_loaded!`/`@loaded_locales` in translate_accelerator compares symbols (`config.locale`). This results in the same locale being loaded twice or not matched at all, and `uniq` failing to dedupe 'de' vs :de. Normalize with `locale.to_sym`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify inconsistent String vs Symbol locale handling as the underlying issue, which can cause the same locale to be loaded twice, and recommend normalizing locales to symbols.

false_positives.candidate:
nil default_locale raises NoMethodError in fallback list

`SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` is called before `.compact`, so if `SiteSetting.default_locale` is nil (or SiteSetting is unavailable, e.g. during asset precompile/early boot or a misconfigured site), `nil.to_sym` raises NoMethodError and every translation lookup through the fallback chain blows up. Guard the value (e.g. `SiteSetting.default_locale.presence&.to_sym`) before calling to_sym, and compact before uniq.

Translation LRU cache key ignores fallback chain / site default locale (multisite leakage)

With fallbacks enabled, a translation result now depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale` in addition to `config.locale`, but the cache key is only `key + config.locale + backend.object_id`. The LRU cache is process-wide, so in multisite (or after changing the site's default locale) a value resolved via one site's fallback chain will be served to another site/request with a different default locale, producing wrong-language strings. Include the fallback chain (or site identifier) in the cache key, or clear the cache when default_locale changes.

Fallback locales only loaded in web requests

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is invoked solely from ApplicationController#set_locale. Code paths that set I18n.locale outside a controller (Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console) will have the fallback locales unloaded, so lookups that should fall back to the site locale or :en will return missing-translation output instead. Loading should be hooked where locale is set globally (e.g. inside the patched translate/load path).

Hash subclass only overrides #[], other Hash API returns empty

`FallbackLocaleList` subclasses Hash but overrides only `#[]`; `fetch`, `keys`, `each`, `empty?` etc. still reflect an empty hash. Any I18n (or plugin) code that uses those methods on `I18n.fallbacks` will see no fallbacks, silently bypassing this feature. Also, defining it at top level without a namespace risks constant collisions.

false_positives.candidate:
strategy.close() destroys the factory-shared queue pool, breaking rebalances

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but the `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared across every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo closes/recreates the strategy on every partition rebalance, so after the first revoke the pool's worker threads are dead and its queues are shut down, while `factory.queue_pool` is still non-None. The next `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` will happily build a strategy over the dead pool and every submitted message will be silently dropped (or raise on `put` into a shut-down queue), stalling the consumer until the process is restarted.

commit function invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ends up in arroyo's `Commit` callback and ultimately the Kafka consumer. Arroyo strategies are documented as being driven from the single processing thread; the underlying consumer and the processor's offset bookkeeping are not thread-safe. Concurrent `commit()` from this thread while the main loop polls/commits can corrupt offset state or raise from librdkafka, risking duplicate or lost processing.

OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition revocation

`OffsetTracker` lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool`, and there is no API to drop state for revoked partitions. After a rebalance, `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` still contain entries for partitions this consumer no longer owns, so the commit thread can emit commits for partitions owned by another member, and stale `last_committed` values for a re-assigned partition can suppress legitimate commits (the loop only commits offsets greater than `last_committed`, which may now be far ahead of the new fetch position).

queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were added in Python 3.13. On any earlier interpreter, `except queue.ShutDown` in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` raises `AttributeError` when an exception propagates, and `q.shutdown(...)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` raises `AttributeError` which is swallowed by the bare `except Exception`. The result is that workers block forever in `work_queue.get()` (the `self.shutdown` flag is only checked between items), so shutdown takes 5s per worker and in-flight work is abandoned. If 3.13 is a hard requirement it should be stated; otherwise use a sentinel item plus `get(timeout=...)`.

Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim

The docstrings for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` and `FixedQueuePool` claim "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but the queues are created as unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. A slow `result_processor` therefore causes unbounded growth of queued `WorkItem`s (each holding the full Kafka `Message`), leading to OOM rather than backpressure, and the comment is misleading. Give the queues a maxsize and raise `MessageRejected` when full.

Lock creation relies on CPython dict atomicity

`_get_partition_lock` does an unsynchronized `get` followed by `setdefault` on a plain dict. This happens to be safe only because of CPython's GIL making `setdefault` atomic; it is not guaranteed by the language and would break under a free-threaded build. Prefer a single module-level lock guarding lock creation, or a `defaultdict(threading.Lock)` created once under a lock.

Transaction name hardcodes 'monitors' prefix for remote subscriptions worker

The sentry transaction name is `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`, but this is generic remote-subscription/uptime code. Including `worker_id` also produces high-cardinality transaction names (one per queue). This will make the uptime consumer's traces show up under misleading `monitors.*` names.

Kafka integration test drives StreamProcessor via private APIs and sleeps

`test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` calls `processor._run_once()` / `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo APIs that can change without notice) and busy-loops for a fixed 5 seconds, which makes the test both brittle against arroyo upgrades and slow/flaky under load. The `commits_made` assertions are also guarded by `if commits_made:` so they silently no-op if no commit was recorded.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.

OptimizedCursorPaginator allows negative offsets, exposing data outside pagination bounds / 500s

The `enable_advanced_features` branch passes `cursor.offset` (negative) directly into a Django queryset slice: `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for negative slice bounds, so any user-supplied cursor with a negative offset yields an unhandled 500 instead of a 400. The accompanying comments ("underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level") are factually wrong; there is no permission check in this code path. Previously negative offsets were effectively bounded; this change removes that safety. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`.

Also, later code still compares `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` using the unclamped `offset`, so when clamping occurs the extra-row trim check no longer matches and an extra row can leak into the page. Either clamp uniformly and use the clamped value in the comparison, or raise on negative offsets.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in BasePaginator.get_result(): when cursor.is_prev is True, start_offset is set to the raw offset without clamping, so a negative offset can be passed into queryset slicing. The candidate adds a secondary related concern about the unclamped offset in the length comparison, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Hardcoded 1000-span cap silently drops spans and ignores max_segment_spans config

Eviction uses a literal `1000` instead of the configurable `max_segment_spans` (1001 in SpansBuffer), and `zpopmin` silently discards the oldest spans with no metric or log. The previous behavior (dropping the whole oversized segment with `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` + error log) was observable; now data loss is invisible. Pass the limit in as an ARGV and emit a metric/return the number evicted.

span_count may be stale, causing over- or under-eviction

`span_count` is set from the result of `zunionstore` calls, but when both unions run the second overwrites the first, and in either case the count reflects the set state before the Python-side `zadd` of new payloads in this batch happens relative to other pipeline commands. Only when `span_count == 0` is `zcard` consulted. If a union ran, the count can be lower than the actual cardinality, so a segment can exceed the cap, or (if a union inflated the count) spans can be evicted unnecessarily. Always read `zcard set_key` right before the cap check.

Redirect-chain loop limit reduced 10000 -> 1000 without justification, and explanatory comment removed

The loop bound was lowered from 10000 to 1000 and the comment warning that chains deeper than the bound may not be joined correctly was deleted. Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects will now silently fail to merge, producing split segments. This is unrelated to the eviction change; if intentional it needs a metric/alert and a comment, otherwise restore 10000.

max_segment_spans is now dead config while enforcement moved to a Lua literal

`self.max_segment_spans` is still a constructor parameter but no longer used anywhere after the span-count check was removed from `_load_segment_data`; the limit is hardcoded as 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Operators tuning `max_segment_spans` will have no effect, and the two values (1001 vs 1000) disagree. Wire the parameter through to the script or remove it.

zadd keyed on payload: duplicate payloads collapse and score is overwritten

Switching from `sadd` to `zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise})` makes the payload the sorted-set member. Two spans with byte-identical payloads still collapse to one entry (same as the set), but now re-ingesting a span also rewrites its score, which changes its eviction priority. More importantly, eviction by `zpopmin` on `end_timestamp_precise` drops the *earliest-ending* spans — typically the root/parent spans of a segment — rather than the least useful ones, which can destroy segment structure. Worth documenting/justifying, and the module docstring (lines 39-44, 58) still describes these keys as "sets" with `sadd` semantics.

__reduce__ omits new/existing fields, so pickled buffers lose configuration

`__reduce__` only passes `assigned_shards`, the two timeouts and `redis_ttl`, dropping `segment_page_size`, `max_segment_bytes` and `max_segment_spans`. In multiprocessing mode the buffer is pickled to subprocesses, so any non-default values for those limits are silently reset to defaults in workers.

No test for the new eviction-during-insert behavior

The PR's stated purpose is eviction during insert, but tests only add the now-required `end_timestamp_precise` field. There is no test that inserts more than the cap into one segment and asserts which spans are retained/evicted, nor a test that the removed `max_segment_spans` read-path behavior is covered by the new Lua cap. Regressions in the eviction arithmetic (stale `span_count`, off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`) would go undetected.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new public paginator wired into a production endpoint but has no unit tests covering next/prev cursors, negative offsets, or the datetime key path. Given it duplicates ~60 lines of `BasePaginator.get_result` with subtle differences, untested divergence is likely.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching allowlist eligibility makes upsampling decisions stale and never invalidated

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the allowlist eligibility result in the shared cache for 60s keyed by org + project set. The `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option lookup it is 'optimizing' is already an in-process/option-store cached read, so the added cache buys little while introducing up to 60s of wrong aggregations (count() silently becoming sum(sample_weight) or vice versa) after the allowlist changes. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but never called anywhere, so there is no invalidation path. Recommend dropping the cache layer entirely.

Shared cache makes the new endpoint tests order-dependent/flaky

Because eligibility is stored in the process-wide cache, the new tests in tests/snuba/api/endpoints/test_organization_events_stats.py that patch `options` (allowlisted / partial / empty) can read a value cached by a previously run test for the same org+project key, producing wrong counts and intermittent failures. Tests would need explicit cache clearing, or the cache should be removed.

Substring match on 'event.type:error' matches negated filters

`_is_error_focused_query` does `"event.type:error" in query`, which is also true for `!event.type:error` (exclude errors) and for `event.type:error_something`. A discover query that explicitly excludes errors would then be transformed to sum(sample_weight), returning inflated/incorrect counts for non-error rows. Parse the query or at least require the term not be negated.

Error-focus detection ignores the query actually executed

`_is_error_focused_query` reads `request.GET['query']`, but the discover-split code path in organization_events_stats mutates the query (e.g. `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction` / `AND event.type:transaction`). The upsampling decision is therefore made from the original user query and can disagree with the query that is run. The effective query string should be passed into the helper.

upsampled_count declares result type 'number' but returns an integer and has no null handling

The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction wraps `sum(sample_weight)` in `toInt64` yet declares `default_result_type="number"`, inconsistent with the sibling count aggregations that use "integer"; clients/meta will report a float type for an integer column. Additionally, events without `sample_weight` (non-upsampled events that may still be in an allowlisted project, or historical data) sum as 0/NULL, silently under-counting; a `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))`-style fallback would be safer than relying on the schema assumption stated in the comment.

Stray git submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed

The PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d2909 with no corresponding .gitmodules entry. This leaves the repository with a broken/uninitializable submodule and is clearly accidental; it should be removed before merge.

Broad silent excepts hide malformed error_sampling context in test factory

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the context lookup and the float conversion in bare `except Exception: pass`. A test that supplies an invalid `client_sample_rate` will silently produce an event without `sample_rate`, making upsampling tests pass/fail for non-obvious reasons. Validate explicitly (e.g. check types / numeric range) and let unexpected input fail loudly.

No test coverage for errors dataset or top-events upsampling paths

The new endpoint tests only exercise the default/discover timeseries path. The code adds upsampling transforms in three places (top_events_timeseries, run_timeseries_query/RPC, timeseries_query); none of the top-events or `dataset=errors` paths, nor the dashboard-widget split path, are covered, so regressions in the alias `upsampled_count() as count` handling for top events would go undetected.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but the permCache entry is set to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}, i.e. a deny, so the assertion assert.False(resp.Allowed) would pass even if the denial cache were not consulted at all. true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous and omits group/resource

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, user UID, action, name and parent folder with '_' separators. Since resource/folder UIDs may legally contain underscores, two different (name, parent) pairs can produce the identical key (e.g. name="a_b", parent="c" vs name="a", parent="b_c"), causing a denial cached for one resource to be returned for a different one. The key also does not include group/resource, so two different group/resource pairs that map to the same action string would share denial entries. The consequence is incorrect (false) denials for up to the cache TTL. Include a non-ambiguous separator/encoding (e.g. length-prefixed or escaped segments) and the group/resource in the key.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug in userPermDenialCacheKey: underscore-separated concatenation can collide when components contain underscores or are empty, causing incorrect denial cache hits. The candidate adds the group/resource omission, but the underlying cache-key ambiguity issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Error from getCachedIdentityPermissions silently swallowed

In Check, the error from getCachedIdentityPermissions is only compared against nil; real errors (e.g. GetUserIdentifiers DB failure or 'unsupported identity type') are indistinguishable from cache.ErrNotFound and are neither logged nor traced. This hides genuine failures and makes debugging cache/identity-store problems hard. Distinguish cache.ErrNotFound from other errors and log/return the latter.

permissionCacheUsage metric counted twice for a single Check

When cached permissions are found but do not grant access, the code increments permissionCacheUsage with label "false" at line 137 after having consulted the cache successfully; conversely a denial-cache hit at line 118 increments "true" and then returns. The 'false' bucket therefore counts cache hits that simply didn't grant permission, so the cache hit-rate metric no longer reflects actual cache hits and will look much worse than reality.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation

remove() now always performs a DB lookup by alias

`idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` is now executed unconditionally at the start of remove(), even when the alias is present in the cache (previously the DB lookup only happened on the invalidated path). `'<%= request.referer %>'` injects an attacker-controlled header directly inside a JavaScript single-quoted string without escaping. A referer containing `'` (e.g. `http://x/'+alert(1)+'`) breaks out of the string and executes arbitrary JS in the Discourse origin. Additionally, postMessage's targetOrigin must be an origin, not a full URL with path/query; derive the scheme+host (e.g. from SiteSetting.embeddable_host) and escape it with `j`/`to_json`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core vulnerability: unescaped request.referer interpolated into inline JavaScript, enabling XSS. The additional postMessage targetOrigin note does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
`force: true` on create_table drops an existing table and its data

Changing `create_table :top_topics` to `create_table :top_topics, force: true` means the migration issues DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before creating. On any installation where this migration already ran (or is re-run), existing top_topics data is silently destroyed. The same pattern is used in the new 20131217174004_create_topic_embeds migration, where re-running would drop all embed mappings. Remove `force: true`.

poll_feed crashes when a feed item has no `content`

`i.content.scrub` assumes every item exposes `content`. For plain RSS 2.0 feeds SimpleRSS exposes `description` and `content` is nil, raising NoMethodError and aborting the whole scheduled job (retry is disabled, so all items are skipped). Fall back to `i.description`/guard against nil. Also `feed_key` is defined but never used, so the HTTP modified-check it implies does not happen.

import mutates the caller's contents string

`contents << "...imported from..."` appends in place to the string passed in by the caller (PollFeed item content, Readability doc content). This mutates caller state, raises RuntimeError on frozen strings, and causes the footer to be appended repeatedly if the same string is passed to import more than once (changing the content_sha1 and triggering spurious revisions). Build a new string instead.

Rails 3 lockfile not updated for new gems

`ruby-readability` and `simple-rss` were added to the Gemfile and to Gemfile_rails4.lock, but Gemfile_rails3.lock was not updated. Booting/bundling in RAILS3 mode (still supported per the Gemfile) will fail with an out-of-date lockfile in deployment/frozen bundles.

Full feed poll executed synchronously inside the retrieve path

`Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` downloads and imports the entire RSS feed inline whenever a single embed URL is missed. For large feeds this makes the retrieve job long-running and can duplicate work across concurrent retrievals (the redis throttle is per embed_url, not per feed).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently overrides the 4-arg version

`def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` (line 145) is immediately redefined by `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` (line 149). In Ruby the second definition wins, so any existing caller passing width and height separately (e.g. `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, w, h, opts)`) now raises ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments, 5 for 3..4), and `downsize(from, to, 100, 100)` would be interpreted as dimensions=100, opts=100. Keep a single method with an unambiguous signature (e.g. accept a dimensions string only, and update all callers).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: self.downsize is defined twice, and the later dimensions-string signature overrides the earlier max_width/max_height signature, breaking callers that pass separate width and height arguments.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

`validateUploadedFile` now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024` KB instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`. Sites configured with a lower (or higher) `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb` will have client validation disagree with the server: attachments larger than the configured limit pass client validation and then fail server-side, and the error message shows the wrong limit. The same hardcoding in the 413 handler (line 246) reports a misleading size to users.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: validateUploadedFile hardcodes maxSizeKB to 10*1024 instead of using Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so client/server limits diverge, and both note the same hardcoding in the 413 handler.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop can spin without progress and still upload an oversized image

The loop calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` up to 5 times but ignores its return value. If the ImageMagick/gifsicle invocation fails (`convert_with` returns false), the tempfile is unchanged and the loop simply burns 5 iterations before passing an image that still exceeds `max_image_size_kb` to `Upload.create_for`. Likewise, 5 × 80% reductions may not be enough for a very large upload, so an oversized image is still accepted. Check the return value, break on failure, and handle the still-too-large case explicitly (error to the user).

Animated GIF detection fails because tempfile paths have no .gif extension

`OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated (gifsicle) code path only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. Here `from` is `tempfile.path`, which for uploaded files is a generic Tempfile path with no image extension, so animated GIFs are processed with `convert #{from}[0]`, which keeps only the first frame and destroys the animation of the user's upload. Pass the original filename/extension or create the tempfile with the proper extension.

API URL download limit hardcoded to 10MB

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces the configurable `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` cap. Sites that intentionally restrict upload size can now have up to 10MB fetched from arbitrary API-supplied URLs regardless of their setting, increasing disk/bandwidth exposure. Derive the cap from a setting instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
unsubscribe_link translation now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking callers that don't supply it

`unsubscribe_link` gained a `%{unsubscribe_url}` interpolation, but `Email::MessageBuilder#body`/`#html_part` interpolate it for every email with `add_unsubscribe_link: true`. A default/fallback or a separate key is needed.

State-changing action exposed over GET without CSRF protection `unsubscribe` mutates the user's notification level but is registered as a GET route (config/routes.rb:440-441) and `check_xhr` is skipped. Mail clients, link scanners, image/link prefetchers, and any third-party page embedding `` can silently mute topics for logged-in users. The unsubscribe should either require a POST/PUT confirmation or be gated by a signed one-time key (like the existing `email/unsubscribe/:key` flow).

301 permanent redirect used for a mutating endpoint

The slug-less `/t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` route redirects with `status: 301`. Browsers and intermediaries cache 301s permanently, so if the topic title (and therefore slug) later changes, clients will keep hitting the stale cached URL. Use 302 here, especially since the target performs a state change.

Email text promises unsubscribe but action only downgrades to regular

The new server locale text says "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here", but the controller only lowers watching/tracking to `regular` on the first click and requires a second visit to mute. A user clicking once will still receive notifications (e.g. for replies to their posts), contradicting the email and the client-side message "You will stop receiving notifications for <topic>".

New unsubscribe route may be shadowed by topic.fromParamsNear

`topic` resource declares child route `fromParamsNear` with path `/:nearPost` under `/t/:slug/:id`, so `/t/slug/123/unsubscribe` can be matched as a topic with nearPost="unsubscribe" depending on route definition order/dynamic-segment matching. Declaring the more specific `topicUnsubscribe` route after the `topic` resource risks the unsubscribe page never rendering (and a bogus post-stream request for post "unsubscribe").

No specs for the new unsubscribe controller action

The new `unsubscribe` action contains non-trivial branching (slug redirect, level toggle, missing TopicUser) and is reachable by any logged-in user via a GET link in emails, yet no request/controller spec was added. Regressions such as the nil TopicUser crash or wrong notification level transitions would go undetected.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The handler looks up the credential with `userId: user.id` only and throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")` when not found. A plain Error surfaces to tRPC as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) rather than NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN, so the client cannot distinguish auth failure from a real server error and the error is logged as an unexpected exception. It should throw `TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" | "FORBIDDEN" })`. Additionally, credentials owned by a team/organization or delegation credentials (userId null or different owner) can never be cleared through this endpoint even though the UI shows the action.

true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: Intl.DateTimeFormat hardcodes the 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, causing the timestamp to ignore locale/time preferences.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache deletion does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query

On successful `deleteCache`, only the optional `onSuccess` callback is invoked; unlike the disconnect mutation (which invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `viewer.apps.integrations` in onSettled), no query invalidation happens. Since `connectedCalendars` is fetched with `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`, the dropdown continues to show the old "Last updated" timestamp and the delete option after the cache was deleted, until a full reload. Cache status never resolves for delegation credentials

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` queries CalendarCache by `credentialId`, but in-memory delegation credentials have synthetic negative ids and their cache rows are looked up by `userId` only (see getCachedAvailability's isInMemoryDelegationCredential branch). For delegation-based connections `cacheUpdatedAt` will therefore always be null and the UI will claim there is no cache even when one exists.

updateManyByCredentialId with empty data on every cache refresh

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` issues an UPDATE on every selected calendar of the credential each time availability is cached, solely to bump `updatedAt`. This value is not consumed anywhere in the UI (the UI uses CalendarCache.updatedAt), so it is a write amplification on a hot path (webhook handling / cron cache refresh) with no consumer. It also touches rows for calendars not involved in the refresh, and is a no-op for delegation credentials with negative ids. Either remove it or restrict it to the calendars actually refreshed.

dev:cron switched to npx tsx without adding tsx as a dependency

`"dev:cron": "npx tsx cron-tester.ts"` relies on `npx` fetching `tsx` from the network at runtime since `tsx` is not listed in dependencies/devDependencies (while the now-unused `ts-node` remains). This breaks offline/CI usage and pins no version. Add `tsx` as a devDependency (and drop ts-node if unused).

Migration warning comment contradicts the actual statement

The generated warning says the column is added "without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty", but the statement does add `DEFAULT NOW()`. Leaving the stale warning is misleading to reviewers/operators evaluating migration safety; it should be removed or corrected.

No tests for new deleteCache handler or cache status enrichment

The new mutation performs a destructive `calendarCache.deleteMany` based on a user-supplied credentialId, and `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` feeds UI state, yet neither has unit tests covering authorization rejection (credential belonging to another user), deletion scope, or the credentialId→updatedAt mapping. Given the authorization-sensitive nature of the endpoint, tests should be added.

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` computes `end` from the slot *start* instead of `slotEndTime`. As a result the check `end > workingHour.endTime` can never detect a slot whose end extends past the end of working hours, so bookings that overrun the organizer's availability are still offered. It should be derived from `slotEndTime`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === (always false)

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two distinct Dayjs object references, which is never true. The intended "full-day unavailable override (start == end)" branch is therefore dead code, so zero-length overrides marking a day unavailable are not handled as designed; use `.isSame()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that === compares distinct Dayjs object references and is always false, recommending .isSame() for the start/end comparison.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours filter rejects slot if any single working-hours entry doesn't contain it

The `workingHours.find(...)` predicate returns true for the first entry that does not contain the slot (different day or different time block), and any truthy result makes the function return `false` (unavailable). With multiple availability rows (e.g. split hours 9-12 and 14-18, or several day groups) virtually every slot matches some non-containing entry and is wrongly marked unavailable. The logic must be inverted: the slot is unavailable only if *no* working-hours entry contains it.

Override day comparison mixes server-local and UTC formatting

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` formats in the server's local timezone while `slotStartTime.format(...)` is UTC (`time.utc()`). On any server not running in UTC the day strings can differ, so overrides are matched to the wrong day (or not matched), making slots wrongly available/unavailable depending on deployment timezone. Both sides should be computed in the same, explicit timezone.

Override timeZone may be undefined, silently falling back to server local time

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is called with `override.timeZone` typed as optional (`TimeRange.timeZone?: string`). When undefined, dayjs falls back to the server's local zone, producing an incorrect `organizerUtcOffset` and therefore shifting date-override slots by an arbitrary amount. Guard with a required timezone or an explicit UTC default.

Override start/end converted to minutes-of-day loses day boundary crossings

`startTime`/`endTime` are computed as `hour()*60 + minute()` after applying the invitee/organizer offset. If the offset pushes the override past midnight (common for large timezone differences) the resulting minute-of-day wraps, so endTime can become smaller than startTime (or 0 for midnight) and the override yields no slots or a bogus range. The conversion needs to account for day overflow (e.g. add 1440 when the date shifts).

New timezone override assertion can pass with missing slots

The `toHaveTimeSlots` matcher only iterates the *actual* slots with `.every` and never compares array lengths, so a result containing a subset (or zero) of the expected slots for that date passes. The newly added `+6:00` timezone assertion therefore does not actually guarantee the date-override timezone fix; add a length/exact-array comparison.

The golden comment and candidate both point to the same underlying problem: invalid computed property keys in the Zod schema that cause fields to be stripped.

Because of the optional chaining, when the value is `null` all collected `teamDestinationCalendars` are discarded, so co-hosts get no calendar event — exactly the case this PR aims to fix. Initialise an array instead.

loadUsers rewrite drops organization select and the no-user guard for dynamic bookings

The new dynamic-user query no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`, which the previous version included and which downstream code uses (e.g. for org-aware booker URLs/links). Additionally, there is no check that the queried users actually exist/match `dynamicUserList.length`, so a booking for a non-existent username now proceeds with fewer (or zero) users instead of failing clearly.

Recurring cancellation now deletes each event once per calendar reference

The recurring branch (which already loops over all of the user's calendar credentials and all updated bookings) is now nested inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With N calendar references the same delete requests are issued N times, multiplying API calls to the calendar providers and producing repeated 404/410 handling. The recurring handling should be hoisted out of the per-reference loop.

Inconsistent destinationCalendar expectations across webhook tests

BOOKING_REJECTED now expects `destinationCalendar: []` while BOOKING_CREATED (line 119) and BOOKING_REQUESTED (line 373) still expect `null`. Since `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` is now an array type, these payloads are shape-dependent on which code path built the event; the inconsistency makes the contract ambiguous for webhook consumers and leaves the array-with-multiple-hosts case untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async callback in forEach: deletions not awaited and errors escape try/catch

Changing the `forEach` callback to `async` means the loop returns immediately; the calendar/video deletions are fire-and-forget. The surrounding `try/catch` can no longer catch failures (rejections happen after the catch block has been left), so errors become unhandled promise rejections instead of being logged, and the function proceeds to send the reschedule email (and returns) before the external events are actually deleted. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
import() invoked eagerly at module load defeats lazy loading

The object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")` etc. immediately when `packages/app-store/index.ts` is evaluated, so every app module is still loaded (and its side effects run) on first access to the app store. The only change versus static imports is that consumers must now `await`; there is no code-splitting or startup-time benefit. To actually defer loading, the values must be thunks (`applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and call sites must invoke them. Additionally, if any of these module evaluations rejects, the stored promise has no attached handler at creation time, producing an unhandled promise rejection that can crash the Node process even if no code ever reads that app.

getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in `calendar`, breaking other consumers

`getCalendar` is now async, so `getCalendarCredentials()` returns items whose `calendar` field is a `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`. Any other caller of `getCalendarCredentials` that uses `.calendar` directly (e.g. truthiness checks or method calls) will now silently treat a promise as a calendar object, and a rejected promise that is never awaited becomes an unhandled rejection. All consumers of this return shape need auditing/updating.

async callback in forEach: deletions not awaited and errors escape try/catch

The `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` callback returns a promise that nobody awaits, so the external calendar/video deletions run detached. The enclosing `try/catch` no longer captures their failures (they surface as unhandled rejections), and the email is sent and the function returns before deletion completes. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`.

requestReschedule deletions are fire-and-forget after making callback async

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` is not awaited, so calendar event deletion / meeting deletion now happen after the tRPC mutation has already responded. Failures become unhandled rejections with no logging, and in serverless environments the process may be frozen before the deletes complete, leaving orphaned calendar events. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`.

Recurring-booking calendar deletes pushed into apiDeletes after it is already awaited

In the recurring branch the callback passed to `forEach` is `async` and awaits `getCalendar(credential)` plus `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` before `apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent)`. Because `forEach` does not await, control returns immediately and `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line 652) runs with an `apiDeletes` array that is still empty for these entries. The recurring calendar deletions are therefore neither awaited nor error-handled; with the extra `await getCalendar` introduced here the race is now guaranteed rather than incidental. Collect the promises synchronously (e.g. `for ... of` with awaited getCalendar, pushing the unawaited deleteEvent promise).

Noisy log.info of CalendarService constructor on every calendar resolution

`log.info("calendarApp", calendarApp.lib.CalendarService)` runs on every call to `getCalendar`, which is on the hot path for availability, booking creation and cancellation. It serializes a class constructor into logs on every request, adding noise and overhead with no diagnostic value. This looks like leftover debug output and should be removed or downgraded to debug.
